items.title: Containment Is Lying to You: Measuring AI Agents Like Employees — Druid AI
items.description:
Two AI interns. One handles 96% of conversations alone, the other only 80%. The dashboard picks the wrong one.

Druid AI's team, including co-founder and chief product officer Dan Bălăceanu, shows why containment rate, the metric on every agent dashboard, can point you to the wrong agent. In their bank example, the intern who escalated more often was handing senior bankers customers who were about to refinance. They walk through a performance review framework built with their customers: seven pillars split into what the agent is configured with and what it does at runtime, with governance across both. Twenty-six components are each scored 0, 1 or 2 (missing, defined, or actually governed and tracked over time) and weighted by business impact, with governance and mandate weighted highest. They cover error tolerance, risk, compliance, observability, drift, hallucination, tone and sentiment, the agent's mandate, scope, business case and budget, a shared platform, and validating outcomes. They also show a dashboard that stays green all year while the agent's real score slides from 83% to 60%, how to answer the ROI question, and why containment targets differ by industry in Druid's 2026 AI Adoption Benchmark.

In this talk:
• Why containment rate can reward the wrong agent
• A seven-pillar scorecard: configuration, runtime and governance
• Scoring and weighting 26 components by business impact
• Answering ROI and setting industry-specific targets

items.title: Stop Renting Intelligence: The Train-to-Deploy Loop for Specialized AI — Fireworks AI
items.description:
Closed models are getting expensive fast. Open models can match them, if you keep training them on your own data.

Jetashree Ravi, who leads part of the applied machine learning team at Fireworks AI, explains how teams move from closed models to open ones without losing quality. Her three truths: open models like GLM 5.2 are production-ready, customization closes the remaining quality gap, and the AI stack is shifting to a continuous train-and-serve loop. She shares Fireworks' scale (about 30 trillion tokens, 10,000+ companies) and customer results: Cursor's Composer 2 trained and hosted on Fireworks with 13x faster inference, a 40x latency improvement for Vercel, and 12% better quality for Genspark with reinforcement fine-tuning. She covers the FireAttention engine and its custom CUDA kernels, speculative decoding with custom draft models, and three ways to train (a training agent, managed training, and a training API for SFT, RFT and DPO), then the flywheel: one-click deploys, monitoring, hot-loading new weights with no downtime, and matching numerics between training and serving. She ends with demos of the training agent and managed training.

In this talk:
• Why open models plus customization can match closed ones
• FireAttention, custom kernels and speculative decoding
• Training agent, managed training and the training API
• Hot loading and numerical fidelity for a continuous train-and-deploy loop

items.title: The Autonomous Computer: Infrastructure for Computer Use Agents — Ang Li, Simular
items.description:
A computer agent finds a speaker on Tuesday's conference schedule, saves the successful steps as a skill, and tries to replay them for Wednesday. A hiccup pushes it back into model driven exploration before the workflow completes. Ang Li uses that demonstration to explain Simular's approach to autonomous computers: combine adaptable vision agents with reusable automation code, then check the environment as each step runs. The workshop traces Agent S from accessibility based control to visual grounding, multiple models, and parallel attempts. It also asks a different reliability question from getting one successful result: can the same agent complete the task repeatedly when prompts and environments vary?

Li demonstrates a coding agent opening the AI Engineer website, reading an accessibility snapshot, and producing a summary. He then connects code replay and recovery to the tension between stability and adaptation, showing where a fixed script can break and where a model can help repair it. The infrastructure discussion moves from an agent occupying a personal desktop to fleets of cloud computers controlled through an interface or API. Recorded examples include legacy form entry and Android interactions. Audience questions examine screen understanding, verification loops, irreversible actions, operating system restrictions, and workflows built from internal procedures. The session presents an experimental direction with visible limitations: benchmark progress and successful demos still leave substantial work in making everyday computer use reliable.

items.title: Hill-Climbing Skills: Improve Agents Without Changing the Model — Shubhankar Srivastava, Browserbase
items.description:
An agent succeeds at a flight search, then fails on its next iteration. Shubhankar Srivastava uses that uneven progress to show how browser agents can learn a task without changing model weights. His AutoBrowse loop pairs a doer that operates the browser with a teacher that reads screenshots, traces and results after each run. The teacher writes lessons into a strategy file, and the next attempt starts with those lessons instead of starting from zero. The flight demo discovers that a URL can encode the search directly, avoiding repeated calendar clicks and an awkward time filter.

The final artifact is a skill file that future agents can reuse. Earlier runs on a conference schedule and restaurant search show how the file preserves navigation choices, waiting behavior and site specific constraints, while replays make the claimed results inspectable. Srivastava then explains what another domain would need to use the same approach: an environment that can be replayed and an outcome that can be verified. Questions expose the limits of that requirement, especially when finding an acceptable flight is easier to judge than finding the best one. The discussion explores task specific versus general skills, different optimization goals, iteration costs and how to measure the verifier itself. For changing websites, he describes monitoring and failure triggered repair loops that produce changes for human review. Prompt injection adds another constraint: generated skills need scrutiny alongside controls on inputs, allowed actions and destinations.

items.title: Taming the AI Hardware Cambrian Explosion — Abdul Dakkak, Modular
items.description:
Compute is booked out for years and new chips keep arriving. The hard part is software that runs well on all of them.

Abdul Dakkak, chief scientist at Modular, explains why today's AI software stack is a mess, with vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and llama.cpp each patching around different hardware, and how Modular rebuilt the stack from the ground up. Mojo is a Pythonic systems language for CPUs, GPUs and accelerators that aims to match CUDA's performance; Modular has open-sourced its kernels, including matmul and attention kernels he says beat the vendor libraries and FlashAttention 4, with Mojo 1.0 and an open-source Mojo coming. MAX is an inference framework that rethinks PyTorch-era assumptions, supports thousands of model architectures behind OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and runs across GPUs, nodes and even mixed hardware. Modular Cloud ties it together as a tunable glass box. He shares benchmarks (Kimi K2.5, FLUX.2, AMD MI355 and Gemma 4), sub-second image generation, and how to try it with pip install modular.

In this talk:
• Why the explosion of AI hardware broke the software stack
• Mojo: Pythonic, portable, and as fast as CUDA
• MAX: inference across GPUs, nodes and mixed hardware
• Benchmarks vs vLLM and torch.compile, and sub-second image generation

items.title: Parameter Golf with AutoResearch — Vayum Arora, Zhengyao Jiang, Dixing Xu & Dhruv Srikanth, Weco AI
items.description:
An agent keeps the code changes that improve a language model's score and discards the rest. Weco AI turns that research loop into a workshop, using Mini Parameter Golf to make training experiments small enough to inspect as they run. Zhengyao Jiang introduces autoresearch as repeated proposals and evaluations, and Dixing Xu explains the team's Aiden system and its contributions to OpenAI's Parameter Golf challenge. Vayum Arora and Dhruv Srikanth then connect those results to a practical setup that combines a modifiable source file, a fixed evaluation command and a measurable goal.

The walkthrough focuses on what determines whether the search is useful: fast and stable evaluations, a clear direction for the metric, time limits, initial guidance and protection against reward hacking. Weco's experiment tree makes each attempt inspectable, with its code changes and score visible in the dashboard. The presenters show how to branch from promising work and steer a running search toward a different idea instead of simply letting it continue. Internet problems lead to a guided setup demonstration, followed by questions about reinforcement learning and combining multiple objectives. The final exercise swaps model training for a Flappy Bird controller scored across normal play, moving gaps, wind and mixed conditions. A hidden validation set and limits on what the controller can edit make the competition another lesson in designing an evaluation that rewards the behavior you want.

Burn Your Flags: Interactive CLIs for Agents — Mark Lummus & Navinkumar Patil, PayPal
items.description:
An agent can miss an interactive terminal prompt without producing an error. The human sees a question and arrow key options; the agent sees a redraw loop and loses the interface state. PayPal's Mark Lummus and Navinkumar Patil use that failure to challenge the standard fix of adding more command flags. Flags work when inputs are independent and the path is known in advance. They become awkward when later questions depend on earlier answers or live API responses. Interactive workflows already contain guidance, choices and guardrails that an agent should be able to follow.

The workshop puts that idea into practice with Barista 9000, a coffee ordering CLI that participants adapt for an agent, with a leaderboard and a Mac Mini prize. Patil introduces three approaches: tmux sessions for sending keys and capturing terminal state, IPC side channels that expose structured JSON instead of screen scraping, and context injection that makes options and constraints explicit. Lummus also asks participants to try less expensive models rather than brute force the task with maximum reasoning. Audience solutions push the benchmark toward deterministic parsers and very low response latency, prompting a discussion of what the competition actually rewards. The closing lesson is to keep the CLI predictable while giving the agent enough context and access to navigate its decisions.

items.title: Build with Perception Agents — Emile Baizel & Shruti Arora, Amazon AGI Lab
items.description:
A coding agent says it added a duck icon to a podcast page; a browser verification pass checks whether the change actually appeared. That audience demo captures the loop Emile Baizel and Shruti Arora build around two perception agent primitives. Visual annotation lets a person select an element, draw on the page or drop a pin, then export structured feedback for a coding agent. Visual verification checks the rendered site against design expectations and user flows. The annotation step is deterministic and produces JSON; the verification step gives the agent a way to inspect the result of its work.

Arora starts from a podcast landing page whose heading, colors and buttons need changes, then connects the browser extension to a coding agent through a local bridge. Participants modify the extension's permissions and add an Apply Changes button, turning exported feedback into a workflow that edits the code, runs verification and produces a report. Easy and medium paths let them follow the wiring directly or solve more of the integration themselves. A guest demonstration uses a simulated Bee conversation as another source of design feedback, feeding the same edit and verification loop. Audience examples extend the idea to spoken feature discussions, project planning and recorded UI feedback, with several integrations still at the concept stage. The closing discussion keeps the focus on making collaboration visual and checking the rendered result, rather than accepting a coding agent's claim that the change is done.

items.title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Javier Garza, Snyk
items.description:
An AI bill of materials turns a repository into a searchable inventory of models, datasets and agents. Javier Garza demonstrates the workflow from a CLI scan to a visual dashboard, then asks it which models the project uses. That inventory anchors a broader security problem: teams cannot assess the AI components they do not know are there. The workshop connects shadow AI to prompt injection, supply chain risk, sensitive information disclosure and excessive agency, using Gandalf challenges and malicious instructions embedded in external content to show how an application's intended rules can be bypassed.

Garza works through defenses at several layers. A database view can restrict what an assistant is allowed to retrieve; limited permissions, output validation and human approval constrain what it can do next. Threat modeling maps assets, trust boundaries and possible attacks before deployment, with an intentionally vulnerable student assistant offered for practice. For skills and MCP servers, he separates scanning tool definitions for hidden instructions from scanning the underlying code for vulnerabilities, then explains a scan, fix and rescan loop driven by coding agent rules and hooks. The final sections examine secure prompting, dependency verification, separate development and production environments, IDE configuration and developer review. Governance depends on explaining guardrails as well as enforcing them, because unexplained restrictions invite workarounds. He closes with offensive agent workflows, training resources and challenges that let participants test these ideas themselves.

items.title: Same Model, Different Speed: Why Your Inference Provider Matters — FriendliAI
items.description:
Open-weight models are good enough now. The question is who can run them fast and reliably.

Yunmo Koo, founding engineer at FriendliAI, argues that open-weight models like GLM 5.2 and MiniMax M3 now compete with the best proprietary models. He shows GLM 5.2 and Claude Opus 4.8 building similar tower defense games from one prompt, with GLM 5.2 more than 5.6x cheaper. Then he runs the same model and the same coding agent on two providers: FriendliAI builds a Candy Crush-style game in about two minutes, the other takes more than three. He explains where the gap comes from: prefix caching with cache-aware routing and a GPU, CPU and NVMe cache hierarchy for long, repetitive agent inputs, plus hybrid speculative decoding that adapts to live traffic. He also covers why reliability matters for agents (one failed call can sink a whole run) and shares Kilo Code's results of up to 7x faster responses with fewer errors.

In this talk:
• Why open-weight models are now good enough for many workloads
• Why the same model feels different on different providers
• Prefix caching, cache-aware routing and a tiered KV cache
• Hybrid speculative decoding and why reliability is part of speed

items.title: SonarQube + OpenAI: Agentic Development — Killian Carlsen-Phelan, Sonar
items.description:
A tiny Python project contains a hardcoded API key, a SQL injection path and other deliberately planted issues. Killian Carlsen-Phelan runs it through SonarQube, brings the findings into Codex and asks the agent to fix the vulnerable query. The scan follows user controlled input into database execution; the repair replaces string interpolation with a parameterized query. A verification hook checks the edited code again, putting the security feedback inside the coding loop rather than leaving it for a later failed build or review.

The workshop develops Sonar's guide, verify and solve workflow through a live setup of SonarQube Cloud, its CLI, plugin and MCP server. A secrets detection hook blocks a fake credential in a prompt, while an issue listing skill gives the agent evidence from the project dashboard. Context augmentation supplies coding guidance before generation, and agentic analysis checks edits as they happen. The opening OpenAI introduction separates execution containment from artifact correctness and defines completion through a reviewable change and independent evidence. Questions explore how the hooks can be bypassed, which steps run locally or in a container, and which features depend on organizational access. Killian finishes by adding a new database operation under the same verification loop, showing how the setup supports both fixing existing issues and checking new work.

items.title: Let Your Agent Cook: Using Skills to Evaluate and Improve Your App — Ankur Duggal, Arize AI
items.description:
A financial agent invents answers, repeats tool calls and produces summaries that its own evaluations flag as wrong. Ankur Duggal connects those failures to a coding agent through Arize's CLI and skills, then asks it to investigate traces, change the application and run experiments. The demo begins with an investment question that looks reasonable at the surface but lacks enough context to support its recommendation. Traces reveal the supervisor, specialist agents, model calls and tools underneath that answer. They turn a vague complaint about quality into evidence about the exact steps that failed.

Duggal sets up the CLI profile and skills, then shows the coding agent pulling spans and evaluation results into its local workspace. The investigation uncovers numeric grounding problems, fabricated responses, redundant searches and failures that the agent silently works around. An earlier experiment targets stock queries outside the United States: changing the country context alone is insufficient until the underlying tool is also updated. Dataset, evaluator and experiment skills make those proposed fixes testable rather than a collection of unverified edits. Questions cover local experiment execution, judge models, evaluation costs, sampling and the risk that a coding agent spends its effort on linting instead of the actual defect. The live repair is still running at the close. Duggal recommends human review of proposed changes and evaluations tailored to the application's failures, so later regressions can be detected as traffic and models change.

items.title: AI Apps in a Flash: Ship to GPUs Without Docker — Dean Quiñanola, Runpod
items.description:
Write code, build the image, push it, run it, find a bug, repeat. One loop can take 15 minutes. Runpod Flash cuts it out.

Dean Quiñanola, staff engineer at Runpod, introduces Runpod Flash, which lets you run Python on cloud GPUs as if the GPU were local, with no Dockerfiles, image builds or registry pushes. He covers serverless queue and load-balanced endpoints, endpoints that call each other like local functions, network volumes with warm caching, and live serverless for instant iteration. In a live demo he checks which GPU he's on (an RTX 4090), evolves the same function into text generation and then image generation, installing dependencies on the fly, and deploys it to production with one command that packages and serves the app without Docker. He also shows off a hackathon project that fans experiments out across endpoints, and how to get started.

In this talk:
• Why the Docker build-push-run loop slows AI development
• Live serverless: iterate on cloud GPUs like they're local
• Endpoint-to-endpoint calls, network volumes and warm caching
• Deploying to production with one command, no Docker

items.title: Continuously Improving Agents with Langfuse — Annabell Schäfer & Lotte Verheyden, ClickHouse
items.description:
A frustrated user types in all caps and tells an IT support agent that its answer did not work. Those interactions become signals that a team can find in production traces, rather than anecdotes lost in a chat history. Lotte Verheyden and Annabell Schäfer build that monitoring workflow with Langfuse and a sample support agent called Specs. The application helps a dad with phone questions, and the workshop follows a request through agent observations, model calls and tools to show what a trace needs to contain before it can support useful evaluation.

The hands on setup connects a TypeScript application built on the OpenAI Agents SDK to Langfuse. Schäfer adds a judge evaluator for user disagreement, a code evaluator for all caps and a scope check that compares the user's request with the system prompt. Each evaluator targets the relevant messages through explicit variable mappings, so its score answers a defined question. Seeded production traces then give a coding agent enough evidence to investigate patterns through the Langfuse CLI and skill. The analysis surfaces issues such as unnecessary tool calls, retries, latency and incomplete evaluation coverage, and the presenters explore a proposed code change. The closing discussion places this online monitoring inside a continuous improvement loop: turn observed failures into representative datasets, run offline experiments, check regressions and repeat as real usage changes.

items.title: Build a Platform and Watch It Burn — Michael Forrester, Accenture & Whitney Lee, Datadog
items.description:
A burrito ordering assistant deploys an external container image and exposes a secret recipe from its Kubernetes environment. Michael Forrester and Whitney Lee invite the audience to push that deliberately permissive bot beyond ordering food, then repeat the attacks with infrastructure and AI guardrails. The exercise makes excessive agency tangible: a friendly business story can turn an ordinary chat interface into a route to tools, files and cluster operations. Model refusals also change between attempts, which complicates the live demos and shows why an application's boundaries cannot depend on the model choosing to refuse.

The workshop moves through three configurations. The first leaves the bot exposed; the second adds infrastructure controls, including Kyverno rules restricting image sources and deployment requirements. Intended runtime protections do not consistently stop recipe access, so the presenters distinguish what worked from what still needs fixing. A third environment lets them toggle LLM Guard input and output filtering, comparing a response that exposes sensitive content with one that redacts it, and a request blocked before model processing. A weather tool introduces another trust boundary: its description asks the agent to read internal configuration alongside a legitimate task. OpenTelemetry traces reveal prompts, tool calls and results in Datadog, making that behavior inspectable. The final discussion connects agent security to established CI/CD, identity, network and artifact controls, and asks when an AI workflow has clear boundaries, a worthwhile cost and a verifiable output.

items.title: Managing Collectors at Scale: OpAMP and  Fleet Management (Grafana ❤️‍🔥 OTel Community Call #11)
items.description:
In this episode of the Grafana OTel Community Call, we're joined by Bejal Lewis and Paschalis Tsilias from Grafana Labs to talk about OpAMP, the Open Agent Management Protocol, and what it takes to manage OpenTelemetry Collectors at scale. We'll cover what OpAMP is and why fleet management matters, where the spec stands today (it's still pre-release), and what it was like building production tooling on top of it.

We'll also look at what went into adding the OpAMP extension to Grafana Alloy's OTel Engine, what "GA" means for Grafana Fleet Management versus the maturity of the upstream spec, and where OpAMP is headed next.

Guests:

· Bejal Lewis (https://www.linkedin.com/in/bejal-lewis/)
· Paschalis Tsilias (https://www.linkedin.com/in/tsilias/)

Host:

items.title: HackTheBox - DevHub
items.description:
00:00 - Introduction
00:36 - Start of nmap
01:22 - Looking at the website on port 80, which advertises MCP Inspector on port 6274. Confirming the port is open with netcat since nmap only scanned the top 1000
02:25 - Looking at port 6274, finding MCPJam 1.4.2 which has an easy RCE (CVE-2026-23744), the same exploit covered on the Kobold video
03:21 - Grabbing the PoC off GitHub and editing it to target devhub.htb:6274 with our IP/port
04:17 - Talking about the different netcat versions and the -e flag, swapping in a bash reverse shell, then getting a shell as mcp-dev and upgrading the TTY
06:31 - Dropping an ed25519 key to SSH in as mcp-dev, then ps -ef --forest to review processes: analyst running JupyterLab (token on the command line) and root running the opsmcp server
09:02 - Using ss -lntp to find the two local services (8888 and 5000) and fingerprinting them by the Server header (TornadoServer is Jupyter, Werkzeug is the Flask app)
10:54 - Forwarding port 8888 over SSH, logging into Jupyter with the leaked token, and using Launcher/Terminal to get a shell as analyst (then dropping an SSH key)
13:31 - As analyst, examining the root-owned opsmcp Flask app (/opt/opsmcp/server.py) and using touch /dev/shm/pwned to detect if/when it restarts
15:12 - Reading the source for the hard-coded API key, authenticating to opsmcp with the X-API-Key header, and working out the tools/call request for ops._admin_dump
19:00 - Dumping root's SSH private key with ops._admin_dump (target ssh_keys) and logging in as root

items.title: What Most People Get Wrong About Evolution | Akarsh Kumar
items.description:
A lot of people in AI treat evolution as a dumb fallback, basically random search for when you can't take a gradient. Akarsh Kumar thinks that is wrong. Selection hangs on to partial solutions, so mutations only need to be useful about 1% of the time for the search to keep making progress.

Akarsh is a PhD student at MIT working with Phillip Isola, works with Sakana AI, and is first author of the Fractured Entangled Representation paper with Kenneth Stanley, Jeff Clune and Joel Lehman. He tells Tim Scarfe why the path a learner takes may shape the structure of what it learns, and why that is a different way of looking at intelligence from the statistical one.

Most of the conversation is about ASAL, the method he led for searching whole spaces of artificial worlds. Rather than predict what a rule will do, ASAL runs the simulation and asks a foundation model what happened. Mapped across all 262,144 Life-like rules, the most interesting worlds sit on one small island. Along the way: Game of Life, Lenia (with a clip from its creator, Bert Chan), neural cellular automata, Boids, Particle Life and the emergence of persistence.

The last stretch is Core War, a programming game from the 1980s. Asked cold, LLMs write poor Redcode. Used as the mutation step in an evolutionary loop with a verifier, they produced warriors that, between them, beat or tied 96% of 294 human-written ones. Over repeated rounds the warriors trended towards generalists.

---
